definition: Least-squares support-vector machines (LS-SVM) for statistics and in statistical modeling, are least-squares versions of support-vector machines (SVM), which are a set of related supervised learning methods that analyze data and recognize patterns, and which are used for classification and regression analysis.
details: In this version one finds the solution by solving a set of linear equations instead of a convex quadratic programming (QP) problem for classical SVMs. Least-squares SVM classifiers were proposed by Johan Suykens and Joos Vandewalle. LS-SVMs are a class of kernel-based learning methods.

explainer.lead: Least-squares support vector machines are support-vector-machine variants that solve a set of linear equations instead of a quadratic programming problem. They matter because they make kernel-based classification and regression cheaper to solve.

tiers.eli5: It is a classifier that, instead of solving a hard puzzle the long way, rewrites it as a set of simple equations that can be solved directly.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use LS-SVMs for classification and regression with kernel functions, solving linear equations for the solution. A pitfall is that the least-squares formulation spreads influence across many points rather than yielding the sparse support vectors of classical SVMs.
tiers.paperLevel: Least-squares versions of support-vector machines, proposed by Johan Suykens and Joos Vandewalle, that find the solution by solving a set of linear equations rather than a convex quadratic programming problem; they form a class of kernel-based learning methods. The formulation does not retain classical SVM sparsity.

explainer.example: A team fits an LS-SVM with a kernel to labelled measurements by solving one linear system, then uses the fitted model to classify new measurements.
